title: Bagging & Random Forests 🌲🌲
description: Bootstrap sampling, averaging, feature subsampling, out‑of‑bag error, and why Random Forests dominate.

slides.title: Bootstrap Aggregating (Bagging) 🎒
slides.content:
# Parallel Ensemble

Bagging creates multiple copies of a model by training each on a **bootstrap sample** of the original data — a random sample **with replacement** of the same size.

- Because of replacement, each bootstrap sample contains about 63.2% unique instances; the rest are duplicates.
- The remaining ~36.8% not selected for a given model are called **out‑of‑bag (OOB)** samples.
- Predictions are aggregated: averaging for regression, majority vote for classification.

Bagging reduces variance without increasing bias. It’s especially effective with unstable models like deep decision trees.

slides.title: Random Forest: Bagging on Steroids 🌳🌳
slides.content:
# Adding Feature Randomness

Random Forest takes bagging further: at each split in each tree, it considers only a **random subset of features** (e.g., √p for classification, p/3 for regression). This decorrelates the trees and reduces variance even more.

Key hyperparameters:
- `n_estimators`: number of trees (more = better, but diminishing returns).
- `max_features`: size of the random feature subset.
- `max_depth`, `min_samples_split`, etc., to control tree complexity.

Random Forest can also output **feature importances** (averaged over all trees), a great tool for feature selection.

slides.title: Random Forest in Scikit‑Learn 🐍
slides.codeSnippet:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=1000, n_features=20, random_state=42)
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, max_features='sqrt', random_state=42)
rf.fit(X, y)
print("Feature importances:", rf.feature_importances_[:5])

quizData.question: What is the main purpose of bootstrapping in bagging?

options.text: To create diverse training sets by sampling with replacement
To reduce the number of features

quizData.explanation: Bootstrapping creates varied datasets, promoting model diversity.

slides.title: Out‑of‑Bag (OOB) Error 📊
slides.content:
# Free Validation

For each tree, the OOB samples (those not in its bootstrap) can be used as a validation set. The OOB error is the average error on these samples across all trees.

- It’s an unbiased estimate of generalisation error, similar to cross‑validation, but obtained without extra computation.
- In scikit‑learn, set `oob_score=True` to get OOB accuracy.

This is a handy way to evaluate your Random Forest without needing a separate validation set.

slides.title: OOB Score Example 🐍
slides.content: Get OOB accuracy with a few lines:
slides.codeSnippet:
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, oob_score=True, random_state=42)
rf.fit(X, y)
print(f"OOB Accuracy: {rf.oob_score_:.3f}")

quizData.question: A Random Forest with 1,000 trees will always outperform one with 100 trees.
quizData.explanation: False. Beyond a certain point, adding trees yields diminishing returns and only increases computation. Often 100‑300 trees are sufficient.
